checks: Cold-read the exact frozen statement and proof before opening the source or graph comparisons. The hull of the finite union of compact fibers is compact. Grouping convex combinations by site and then applying the anchored inclusions gives C_z=K_z for each z in P. Affinity of each plane at a fixed u propagates its support-majorant inequality from the generators to all of C. Convexity and continuity of each field on C give closed convex intersections, and field nonnegativity gives nesting.

For an inball of radius r_z about o_z, h_z(u)−u·o_z≥r_z. Consequently the homothet with fractional shrink τ_z=εM/r_z has support at most h_z(u)−εM in every unit direction, enough to satisfy all fields because its points are in C. Finiteness gives a common ε-range with τ_z<1, and M=0 is the constant family. The shrunken inballs put o_z strictly inside each new fiber. Positive fibers over all sites imply that the projection is conv(P), lattice completeness excludes every other integer fiber, and convexity gives the anchored inclusions. The projection spans aff(P) and a positive fiber supplies all continuous directions, also for n=0 or deficient base rank.

Each ray has a unique new endpoint by convexity and the retained inball, with 0≤s_ε≤εM/r_z. For each old active cut at a regular x, substituting the endpoint gives the lower bound after dividing by ε and using continuity, since ν·(x−o_z)≥r_z. For the upper bound, follow a positive limsup along a sequence with s_ε>0. Its new endpoints lie in the old interior. If all cuts were slack there, compactness of the sphere and finiteness of I would yield a positive minimum slack, and joint continuity on the compact sphere times a short old-interior ray segment would let the ray advance. Thus some cut is tight at each such endpoint.

On a subsequence the tight index is constant and its normals converge. Their old slack is bounded by εM+s_ε|x−o_z| and splits into the nonnegative original plane gap and the nonnegative support gap at x. Both vanish at the limit, so the limit normal is the unique old normal and the limit index is an old contact. The radial denominator tends to a number at least r_z, so dropping the old slack gives the upper bound by this contact value, hence by the maximum. This also excludes a positive limsup when there is no old contact and handles changing tight normals without continuity of the contact set.

Convex boundary charts give a measurable unit normal almost everywhere. Each contact equality is measurable there, so the finite contact maximum is measurable. The fractional loss is Borel because s_ε(x)≤t is equivalent to membership of the radial point at fractional depth t in the closed new fiber for 0≤t≤1. The layer map is injective on 0≤s<1 because the center is interior and rays have unique old endpoints. Its tangential scaling is (1−s)^(d−1), and the normal component of the radial derivative has absolute value ν·(x−o_z). The area formula then yields the stated Jacobian. After rescaling s by ε, the layer integral has a fixed upper bound in the rescaled variable and a bounded surface density, so the pointwise limit gives exactly ∫v_z dS by dominated convergence. The argument in d=1 uses the two disjoint endpoint intervals directly.

For a fixed cap, H_z is all of the fiber space, empty, or a closed halfspace. A fully captured K_z gives its whole loss; when its interior is disjoint the trace is at most (d−1)-dimensional and has zero d-volume for both bodies. In the remaining case the cutting plane crosses the interior. If a relative interior point of its section lay on the old boundary, every support there would contain the cutting plane because the section contains a neighborhood in that plane. Such a support is impossible through the body interior. Thus the boundary trace lies in the relative boundary of a full (d−1)-dimensional section and is surface-null. In d=1 the section is a single interior point. Every other boundary point has positive signed-distance margin and its entire sufficiently thin radial layer has the same cap status. The same domination gives the cap formula, and finite sums and maxima give precisely the asserted finite-list uniformity.

Checked two exact examples. On K=[−1,2], use ell=h for both cuts, fields V_1(+1,x)=x+1, V_1(−1,x)=1, V_2(+1,x)=2, V_2(−1,x)=0. For 0<ε<1/2 the new interval is [−1+ε,(2−ε)/(1+ε)], with losses ε and 3ε/(1+ε) and limiting endpoint speeds 1 and 3. The proper cap x≥0 has loss 3ε/(1+ε), the outside trace x≥2 has zero loss, and the inside support x≤2 gives the total. On K=[−1,1]^2 with ell=h and V(u,x)=|u_1|, the new rectangle is [−1+ε,1−ε]×[−1,1] by the two axial cuts and the support comparison in all other directions. Its total loss is exactly 4ε, the cap x_1≥0 loses 2ε, and the outside trace x_1≥1 loses zero despite positive old surface measure.

overlap.comparison: Its first volume variation covers a common full-dimensional polytope with a fixed irredundant finite facet-normal list and perturbations of facet offsets. It agrees with the total loss in the case of constant inward offset speed on each original facet. It has no point-dependent cut field, compact family of normals, or fixed-cap selector for supporting traces.

Its smooth local support bump gives a volume surface integral and exact changes for caps whose planes stay strictly away from the moving patch. It uses one body, d≥2, local C² support and positive curvature, and prescribed smooth support shifts. It does not yield contact-max speed for arbitrary compact convex fibers under finite global cuts or handle supporting traces meeting a moving facet.

Its first variation moves the cap parameters for fixed fibers and integrates over the cutting sections. It requires zero surface measure for nonproper traces. The frozen claim keeps the cap fixed, varies the actual fiber boundary, and includes outside supporting traces of positive surface measure.

readability: The compactness step giving a tight cut and the radial area-formula argument are concise but complete. An optional sentence identifying the Borel sublevel sets of the fractional loss would make measurability explicit. The proof uses the exact radial Jacobian and accounts for the one-dimensional case separately.

summary: The frozen proof establishes exact compatibility for sufficiently small finite global-cut erosions, the pointwise radial speed at every regular old boundary point, and the first total and fixed closed-cap losses. In particular, a supporting trace outside the fiber interior has zero loss even when its surface measure is positive. The argument is self-contained and no accepted fact at 694b9a0 covers the full claim.
